comments.body:
═══ RESULT: NET-POSITIVE. 12 calls → 2, input tokens 17,558 → 9,116 (−48.1%) versus the PRE-8415
baseline, and the prefix now caches (write 1,331 then read). Verdict parity is the honest caveat:
surfaced findings identical 5/5 runs, but relation labels shift on 6/12 ordered pairs. ═══

**METHOD.** One pinned query ticket (`6a89-1165-ea58-4be3`) and its top-6 BM25F candidates, frozen
to a JSON file so every arm sees byte-identical inputs. A recording proxy wraps the real runner in
`judge()` and reads `_usage` off each response. Three builds measured on the SAME corpus rather
than comparing against 8415's differently-sized one:

    A = pre-8415  (judge.py at HEAD~1)     B = 8415 hoist (HEAD)     C = this change

**BEFORE / AFTER, real `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6`.**

                                    A pre-8415   B 8415      C batched
    judge calls                             12          12           2
    stable system prefix (count_tokens)    422         873       1,337    floor 1024
    distinct system prompts                  1           1           1
    input_tokens (total)                17,558      18,494       9,116
    output_tokens                          428         438         599
    cache_write_tokens                       0           0       1,331
    cache_read_tokens                        0           0       1,331
    surfaced findings                       []          []          []

    C vs A (pre-8415):  −8,442 input tokens  (−48.1%)
    C vs B (8415):      −9,378 input tokens  (−50.7%)

The A→B delta reproduces 8415's measurement exactly: **+936 input tokens**, the same number 8415
recorded, and cache_read/cache_write still 0 at an 873-token prefix. So the pair 8415+c403 is
decisively net-positive against the pre-8415 baseline, and 8415's regression is erased.

**THE FLOOR IS CROSSED, AND BY THE MECHANISM PREDICTED — WHICH IS NOT THE ONE THE ORIGINAL PLAN
NAMED.** Batching by itself adds NOTHING to the cacheable prefix: the prefix is the SYSTEM block
(base prompt + hoisted query digest), and extra candidates go in the USER message. What lifted it
is the BATCH PROTOCOL section the prompt now has to carry — `count_tokens` puts it at **+436
tokens** — taking 873 → 1,337. Both halves are visible in the numbers above: the prefix crossing
1024 turns caching on, and the 12 → 2 call reduction is what actually removes the tokens.

    two calls, one batch:  call 1 writes 1,331   call 2 reads 1,331   (exactly one prefix write)

A repeat run confirmed the cache survives between runs: a second batched run over the same corpus
billed `cache_read_tokens: 2,662`, `cache_write_tokens: 0` — both calls read a prefix written by
the previous run, same 9,116 input total.

**COVERAGE OF THE FLOOR ACROSS TICKETS, not just this one.** `count_tokens` over the base prompt
plus a random sample of 12 real corpus digests gave hoisted prefixes of 632–978 — every one under
1024, corroborating 8415's 728–875 range on a different sample. With the +436 batch section every
one of those becomes 1,068–1,414, so the crossing is not specific to this query ticket. Measured,
not extrapolated from a single digest.

**PRE-8415 BASELINE NOTE.** 17,558 here vs 8415's 16,040: different corpus, larger digests
(415–543 tokens each vs 8415's 306–453). That is exactly why all three arms were re-measured on
one pinned corpus rather than compared across tickets.

comments.body:
═══ VERDICT PARITY — reported straight, because it is NOT clean. Surfaced findings are identical
on every run (5/5), but relation LABELS shift on 6 of 12 ordered pairs, reproducibly, and the
shift is mostly toward the conservative end. ═══

**THE CONTROL THAT MAKES THIS READABLE.** A single before/after comparison cannot separate "the
judge is noisy" from "batching changed the judge", so each build was run TWICE on the same corpus
and the within-build churn measured first.

    WITHIN-build churn (identical code, two runs)   B vs B2 per-pair   1 / 12
                                                    C vs C2 batched    3 / 12
    BETWEEN-build churn                             A vs B  (8415)     0 / 12
                                                    B vs C             6 / 12
                                                    B2 vs C2           6 / 12   <- reproduces

6/12 on two independent pairs of runs against a 1–3/12 noise floor: the shift is **systematic**,
not sampling variance. (A vs B at 0/12 also re-confirms 8415's own 12/12 parity claim.)

    pair            A pre-8415        B 8415            B2 rerun          C batched         C2 rerun
    2fd4#first      depends_on        depends_on        depends_on        related_distinct  related_distinct
    2fd4#second     related_distinct  related_distinct  depends_on        related_distinct  depends_on
    4b5b#first      related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct
    4b5b#second     related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct
    e68d#first      related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct
    e68d#second     related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct
    2610#first      related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  unrelated         unrelated
    2610#second     related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  unrelated         unrelated
    9249#first      related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  depends_on
    9249#second     related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  depends_on        related_distinct
    2bbd#first      related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  unrelated         unrelated
    2bbd#second     related_distinct  related_distinct  related_distinct  unrelated         unrelated

    surfaced findings   A []   B []   B2 []   C []   C2 []

**WHAT THE SHIFT IS.** Five of the six divergences move AWAY from surfacing: `2610` and `2bbd`
(four pairs) go `related_distinct` → `unrelated`, and `2fd4#first` goes `depends_on` →
`related_distinct` — the batched judge declines a directional relation the per-pair judge asserted.
Seeing five candidates side by side appears to make the model readier to call a weak neighbour
plainly unrelated, which is the direction a prompt whose own rule is "false flags are costly"
should prefer.

The sixth, `9249`, is the one that moves the wrong way: the batched build asserts `depends_on` in
ONE ordering — `#second` in run C, `#first` in run C2, i.e. it does not even pick the same
ordering twice. It never survives aggregation, because the both-orderings-agree rule downgrades a
one-sided directional claim. This is precisely the case that rule exists for, and it held.

**RECALL — the gap in the above, and the control that closes it.** All five runs surfaced `[]`, so
the corpus contains no true positive and CANNOT distinguish "batching preserves recall" from
"batching surfaces nothing". A positive control was therefore run: the query's own digest injected
as a seventh candidate (a guaranteed `duplicates`) alongside five real negatives, judged on both
builds.

    per-pair (B):  ZZZZ-self#first duplicates/1.0   #second duplicates/1.0
    batched  (C):  ZZZZ-self#first duplicates/1.0   #second duplicates/1.0

    finding, BOTH builds, byte-identical including the cited artifact:
      rebar link 6a89-1165-ea58-4be3 ZZZZ-self-duplicate duplicates
      shared_artifact: docs/adr/NNNN-opcert-asymmetric.md   confidence 1.0

    tokens on that corpus:  per-pair 12 calls / 18,478 in  ->  batched 2 calls / 9,086 in

So the true positive is recovered at full confidence in both orderings, with the same cited
artifact, and the five surrounding negatives did not contaminate it — the cross-contamination this
change risks did not occur on the one true positive available to test.

**HONEST LIMITS.** One query ticket, six candidates, two runs per build, one synthetic positive.
That is enough to show the finding-level output is unchanged and the systematic relation shift is
conservative; it is NOT enough to bound recall loss on real duplicates at scale. A corpus of real
labelled positives would be needed for that, and this repo's store did not supply one for the
query measured.

**MUTATION CHECK.** Restored tree asserted all-pass before AND after the sweep (31 passed, exit 0
both times). Each mutation applied ALONE to `judge.py`, then reverted.

    M1  _CANDIDATES_PER_CALL = 1 (batching defeated)
        -> FAILS test_batching_issues_fewer_calls_than_one_per_ordered_pair,
                 test_a_corpus_larger_than_the_bound_is_split_across_calls,
                 test_shared_query_digest_lives_only_in_the_system_prompt
    M2  demultiplex by POSITION instead of label
        -> FAILS test_batch_verdicts_are_matched_by_label_not_by_position,
                 test_a_missing_or_unknown_batch_entry_abstains_only_that_candidate
    M3  a duplicate entry overwrites the first (seen-guard dropped)
        -> FAILS test_a_duplicate_batch_entry_does_not_overwrite_the_first
    M4  an unknown candidate_id is accepted into the result map
        -> FAILS test_a_missing_or_unknown_batch_entry_abstains_only_that_candidate
    M5  ordering-2 slots collapsed (shared ref FIRST in both orderings)
        -> FAILS test_hoisted_reference_keeps_the_ordered_pair_slots
    M6  candidates listed WITHOUT their [candidate_id: ...] label
        -> FAILS 11 tests, incl. both batching tests and every surfacing test
    M7  judge_batch fail-safe removed (errors propagate)
        -> FAILS test_a_raising_runner_surfaces_nothing_for_a_whole_batch,
                 test_llm_error_abstain
    M8  the batch call stops hoisting the shared digest into the system prompt
        -> FAILS test_shared_query_digest_lives_only_in_the_system_prompt
    M9  an UNLABELLED entry is spread over every candidate in the batch
        -> FAILS test_a_malformed_batch_response_surfaces_nothing[response3]

Every new test is killed by at least one mutation and passes on the restored tree; no mutation
survived. M9 was added after M1–M8 showed the malformed-batch test surviving them all: its
unlabelled-entry case was passing for the wrong reason (the canned verdict cited no
`shared_artifact`, so the artifact rule was doing the work, not the demultiplexer). The case was
strengthened to a fully surfaceable verdict, which M9 then kills. Recorded because a test that
passes for the wrong reason is the failure mode a mutation check exists to catch.

**GATES, by exit code, on a tree asserted CLEAN (`git status --porcelain` empty) immediately
before and immediately after the run:**

    make lint                                                       exit 0
    make typecheck                                                  exit 0
    pytest -m "not integration and not external" -n 6 --dist worksteal   exit 0
        8987 passed, 31 skipped, 583s

Three tests OUTSIDE the declared file budget failed on the first full run and were fixed as
consequences of the change, not worked around:
`test_subcall_class_selection.py::test_overlap_judge_selects_the_standard_class_for_every_pair`
(asserted 4 calls for 2 candidates — now uses `_CANDIDATES_PER_CALL + 1` candidates so it still
spans more than one call, preserving its "the binding holds per call, not only the first" intent),
and the two `test_plan_review_overlap.py` pipeline tests (their canned runner answered in the
single-pair shape; it now echoes the verdict once per labelled candidate).

**COMMIT (local only — NOT pushed to Gerrit, ticket NOT closed):**
`302b07e6ee4c6546a1b3ce8fc249391e2a177895` on `feat/c403-overlap-batch`, worktree
`/Users/joeoakhart/feat-c403-overlap-batch`, based on `bd2cc1c036d` (8415's commit), so it STACKS
on 8415 as the operator directed. Change-Id `I28fc02d0ed3a722326a05b90e3f547593a7721c6`,
DCO-signed as `RebarBotNava <joeoakhart+bot@navapbc.com>`, `rebar verify-commit-ticket` exit 0.
Files: `src/rebar/llm/overlap/judge.py`, `src/rebar/llm/contracts.py`,
`src/rebar/llm/reviewers/overlap_judge.md`, and three test files (+371/−42). `judge.py` is 262
lines, inside the 800 cap.

`src/rebar/schemas/` was NOT touched: `overlap_verdict_batch` is an internal contract with no
`--output` surface (same shape as `plan_review_novelty`), so no schema file is added and the
every-schema-file-is-wired guard is unaffected. `capabilities.py`'s `CACHE_MIN_PREFIX_TOKENS` was
NOT touched (ticket e3cd) — note it still reads 4096, so `warn_if_cache_ineffective` remains blind
to this now-genuinely-caching 1,337-token call site.

compiled_state.description:
# Batch overlap-judge candidates per call: cut call volume, and grow the prefix past 1024

## Context / Problem

Story `8415-b6e8-c206-48f6` moved the batch-invariant query digest out of the per-call user
message into the overlap-judge system prompt, so the shared bytes sit in the block the runner
already puts a cache breakpoint on. That relocation is done and measured. It does not pay off,
because the resulting prefix does not reach the model's minimum cacheable prefix.

Measured on real `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6` calls (the `standard` class `overlap-judge` runs
on post-`afeb`), one query ticket and six candidate digests, 12 calls:

    stable system prefix   before  423 tokens        after  846 tokens      floor  1024
    input tokens           before  16,040            after  16,976          (+936, +5.8%)
    cache_read_tokens      before  0                 after  0
    cache_write_tokens     before  0                 after  0
    verdict parity         relations identical on 12/12 ordered pairs

The floor is measured, not assumed: through the real judge request path an 875-token system
prefix produced write 0 / read 0 while a 1250-token one produced write 1243 then read 1243.
`count_tokens` over the base prompt (423) plus each of seven real `rebar.llm.enrich` digests
(306-453) gives 728-875 — every one short of 1024 by **149-296 tokens**. So the relocation costs
~5.8% more input and returns nothing, and 8415 is held until this ticket makes the pair
net-positive.

## Approach

Judge N candidates in ONE call per ordering instead of one call per candidate per ordering.
Today `judge()` issues 2N calls, each re-sending the whole system prefix. Batched, it issues
`2 * ceil(N / batch)` calls: the query digest stays hoisted in the system block (unchanged from
8415), and the user message carries a LABELLED LIST of candidate digests instead of one.

**Two mechanisms, and they are NOT the same mechanism. State them separately, because one is
arithmetic and the other is a bet.**

1. **Call-count reduction — arithmetic, and the mechanism the ticket actually rests on.** Every
   avoided call removes one whole copy of the 846-token prefix from the bill. At N=6 with one
   batch per ordering, 12 calls become 2: ten prefix copies (~8,460 tokens) disappear outright.
   This requires no caching whatsoever and cannot fail to reduce total input tokens; only its
   magnitude is uncertain, because the candidate digests themselves are re-sent either way.

2. **Prefix growth past 1024 — a bet that must be measured, and batching ALONE does not deliver
   it.** The cacheable prefix is the *system block*: base prompt + hoisted query digest. Putting
   more candidates in the *user* message does not add a single token to it. Batching lifts the
   prefix only because the batch protocol has to be described somewhere, and it belongs in the
   system prompt: per-candidate independence, the labelled-list input shape, one echoed verdict
   per candidate. That section is required by the change, not padding invented to reach a number
   — but whether base 423 + section + digest 306-453 clears 1024 for every real digest is an
   empirical question this ticket answers with `count_tokens`, and it may come out short for the
   smallest digests. A prefix that still does not cache is a valid recorded outcome; mechanism 1
   carries the ticket in that case.

Deliberately NOT done: no padding is added to reach the floor (buying a cache with the tokens it
was meant to save is not a saving), `capabilities.py`'s `CACHE_MIN_PREFIX_TOKENS` is not touched
(that is ticket `e3cd`), and the loop is not parallelized (fanning out cold calls that share a
prefix turns one write plus reads into N premium writes — strictly worse; 8415 records this).

**The cost is precision, and it is a real cost.** `reviewers/overlap_judge.md` is written for ONE
ORDERED PAIR — "FIRST <relation> SECOND", a closed five-value relation set, a required named
`shared_artifact`, `related_distinct` as the default, "false flags are costly". Judging several
candidates in one call risks cross-contamination: a shared artifact cited for one candidate
bleeding into the verdict for another, or an unrelated candidate dragged toward
`related_distinct` by its neighbours. This is the real risk of the change and it is MEASURED, not
asserted, by the parity run below.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/overlap/judge.py` — batch construction (a labelled candidate list, the batch-size
  bound) and per-candidate response demultiplexing. `judge_one` and the un-batched request shape
  stay as the single-pair path, unedited.
- `src/rebar/llm/reviewers/overlap_judge.md` — a BATCH section describing one FIRST against a
  labelled list of SECOND candidates (and the mirrored ordering), per-candidate independence, and
  one echoed verdict per candidate. The single-pair instructions above it are unchanged.
- `src/rebar/llm/contracts.py` — a new `overlap_verdict_batch` contract: a list of per-candidate
  entries, each carrying `candidate_id` plus today's four `overlap_verdict` fields. Registered
  next to `overlap_verdict`, which keeps its registration and its single-pair use.
- `tests/unit/test_overlap_judge.py` — batch payload shape, demultiplexing, and fail-safe tests.

No `src/rebar/schemas/` change: `overlap_verdict_batch` is an internal contract with no `--output`
surface, like `plan_review_novelty` and `code_review_coach`, so no schema file is added and the
every-schema-file-is-wired guard is unaffected. No `config.py` change: the batch bound is a module
constant in `judge.py`, since no operator-facing tuning is claimed for it.

## Testing

Offline tests drive the real `judge()` through the existing recording fake runner, asserting on
the ACTUAL `RunRequest` payload rather than a stand-in.

- **Call count** — 6 candidates yield strictly fewer `RunRequest`s than 12, and each ordering's
  request carries every candidate's digest block, each under its own label.
- **Both orderings survive batching** — in ordering 1 the hoisted reference occupies the FIRST
  slot and the labelled candidate list the SECOND; in ordering 2 the reverse.
- **Demultiplexing** — a canned batched response maps back to exactly one verdict per candidate,
  matched by label and not by position; a candidate absent from the response, and a response
  entry naming an unknown label, both resolve to abstain for the affected candidate only, leaving
  the others' verdicts intact.
- **Fail-safe** — a runner that raises, and a runner returning a malformed batch (not a dict / no
  verdict list / entries missing their label), each yield `[]` from `judge()` with nothing
  propagating.
- **Batch bound** — a corpus larger than the bound is split into multiple calls per ordering, and
  every candidate still receives exactly one verdict.
- **Mutation check, both directions, for every new test:** each new test must FAIL with the
  batching change reverted and PASS restored. Recorded on the ticket.
- **Real-API parity and measurement** — the same query ticket and candidate corpus judged on
  8415's per-pair build and on this batched build, relations compared pair by pair.
- Gates: `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and
  `pytest -m "not integration and not external" -n 6 --dist worksteal -q`, judged by exit code.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The batched build issues strictly fewer calls than candidates x 2 for a corpus of >= 6
      candidates, shown by a recording-runner test counting `RunRequest`s.
- [ ] Every candidate receives exactly one verdict, matched by its label rather than by position;
      an absent or unlabelled entry becomes an abstain for that candidate ONLY; checked by the
      demultiplexing tests.
- [ ] The step stays advisory: a raising runner and a malformed batched response each yield `[]`
      from `judge()` with no exception escaping; checked by the fail-safe tests.
- [ ] Precision is shown, not assumed: a real-API parity run over one query ticket and at least
      six candidates reports per-pair `relation` for the per-pair build and the batched build, and
      any differing relation is called out with its digests; recorded as a ticket comment.
      Identical relations on every pair is the pass condition; a divergence is reported, not
      averaged away.
- [ ] A BEFORE/AFTER measurement on real `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6` calls over the SAME query
      ticket and SAME corpus records, for both builds, total `input_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`,
      `cache_write_tokens`, the call count, and the `count_tokens` size of the stable prefix beside
      the measured 1024 floor.
- [ ] The pair is judged against the PRE-8415 baseline, not just against 8415: the batched build's
      total `input_tokens` must be below **16,040** on the same corpus, or the ticket reports the
      pair as still net-negative in plain terms with the numbers. `cache_write_tokens` above one
      prefix write per batch FAILS this criterion.
- [ ] The prefix bet is reported either way: the batched `count_tokens` prefix is recorded against
      1024 for the corpus's digest-size range, and a prefix that still does not clear the floor is
      recorded as such rather than presented as a caching win.
- [ ] Every new test is mutation-checked in both directions and the evidence recorded as a ticket
      comment.
- [ ] `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and `pytest -m "not integration and not external"` all exit 0.
